nameStory: The rainbow scarab gets its dazzling name from the brilliant metallic sheen that covers its dark body, creating an iridescent display of greens, blues, purples, and bronzes that shifts and shimmers as the beetle moves. Like a tiny living jewel crawling through the forest floor, this beetle's colorful exterior seems almost too beautiful for an insect that spends its life working with dung. The name 'scarab' comes from the ancient Egyptian word for these sacred beetles, though our New England species is far from the deserts of the pharaohs.
description: The rainbow scarab is a stocky, oval-shaped beetle about the size of a large marble, typically measuring around 0.5 to 1 inch long. Despite being a dung beetle, it's one of New England's most beautiful insects, with a dark body covered in brilliant metallic colors that shimmer like an oil slick in sunlight. Males sport impressive horn-like projections on their heads and thorax, making them look like tiny rhinoceros beetles. These industrious insects are nature's cleanup crew, spending their lives burying animal droppings to feed their young.

idTips.label: Metallic Rainbow Sheen
idTips.description: The body gleams with brilliant metallic colors - greens, blues, purples, and bronze - that shift and change as you view it from different angles, like looking at soap bubbles or gasoline on water

idTips.label: Male Horns
idTips.description: Males have prominent horn-like projections on the head and a raised ridge on the thorax, feeling hard and smooth to the touch like polished plastic

idTips.label: Stocky Oval Shape
idTips.description: Body is notably chunky and dome-shaped, about as wide as it is long, with a solid, heavy feel when handled - much more robust than most beetles of similar size

idTips.label: Powerful Front Legs
idTips.description: Front legs are noticeably thick and flattened with tooth-like projections, designed for digging - they feel surprisingly strong and may pinch if the beetle grabs you

idTips.label: Size and Heft
idTips.description: About marble-sized but with surprising weight for its size, typically 0.5-1 inch long and feeling substantial in your palm

idTips.label: Dung Association
idTips.description: Almost always found in or around fresh animal droppings, particularly horse, cow, or deer scat, often with a distinct earthy-musky smell

habitat: Look for rainbow scarabs in open woodlands, pastures, and forest edges where large mammals leave droppings - they're especially common around horse farms, cattle pastures, and deer trails. They prefer areas with loose, well-drained soil that's easy to dig into, from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England. You'll often find them in the same spots where you see deer scat or horse manure, as they need fresh dung to survive and reproduce.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots in late spring and become active when temperatures warm, often found around the first fresh animal droppings of the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively flying to fresh dung and can sometimes be seen on warm evenings attracted to lights.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding and mating into early fall, with some individuals beginning to seek shelter under logs or in leaf litter as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate deep in soil or under debris, completely inactive and hidden until spring warmth returns.

funFact: A single rainbow scarab can bury a pile of horse manure 50 times its own weight in just one night, working as a super-efficient underground recycling team with its mate to turn waste into fertilizer and create nursery chambers for their young.
confusionNotes: Rainbow scarabs might be confused with other metallic beetles like ground beetles or carrion beetles, but remember the 'dung rule' - if it's not in or near fresh animal droppings, it's probably not a rainbow scarab. Their chunky, dome-shaped body and association with scat makes identification much easier.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dung beetles,' rainbow scarabs are actually performing a vital ecological service by rapidly burying and recycling animal waste, preventing fly breeding and returning nutrients to the soil. Ancient Egyptians revered scarab beetles as symbols of renewal and rebirth because they seemed to create life from waste, though the Egyptian sacred scarab is a different species entirely.
compareHints: Rainbow scarabs are the only Phanaeus species commonly found in New England, making them relatively easy to identify within their genus. Compared to other dung beetles in the scarab family, rainbow scarabs are notably larger and more colorful, with much more prominent horns on males. Other New England dung beetles tend to be smaller, less iridescent, and lack the impressive horn structures that make rainbow scarabs look like tiny armored warriors.
